bio.en: Barbra Gago is founder and CEO of Pando, a career-progression platform democratizing promotion and feedback, previously CMO and Global Head of Marketing at Miro and VP of Marketing at Greenhouse.
bio.zh: Barbra Gago 是 Pando 的创始人兼 CEO，Pando 是一个让晋升与反馈更普惠的职业发展平台，此前曾任 Miro 首席营销官兼全球市场负责人，以及 Greenhouse 营销副总裁。

summary.en: Barbra explains category creation—how she rebranded Miro and launched the “visual collaboration” category, and why a similar attempt at Greenhouse failed. She shares why a great brand is informed by its values and why Pando is built as opinionated software for career growth. The conversation covers branding, rebranding, and the strategic decision of when (and when not) to create your own category.
summary.zh: Barbra 讲解了品类创造——她如何重塑 Miro 品牌并推出“可视化协作”品类，以及在 Greenhouse 类似尝试为何失败。她分享了为何优秀品牌由其价值观塑造，以及 Pando 为何作为“有主张的”软件来构建职业发展。对话涵盖品牌、品牌重塑，以及何时（不该）自创品类的战略决策。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: When you're building a category, you need to make sure that there is a category that's validated by analysts and directory sites and things like that. But also, you want to have a lot of traction in terms of thought leadership like why is this the category? What are the unique value propositions of this particular thing? What are the pain points it solves? And then of course, getting a lot of content around because when you're generating a new category, you're also needing to educate buyers that there is a category that they can now budget for and why they should allocate budget for that.
turns.zh: 当您构建类别时，您需要确保有一个类别经过分析师和目录网站等的验证。而且，你希望在思想领导力方面有很大的吸引力，比如为什么是这个类别？这个特定事物的独特价值主张是什么？它解决了哪些痛点？当然，要获得大量内容，因为当你生成一个新类别时，你还需要教育买家，他们现在可以为某个类别进行预算，以及为什么他们应该为此分配预算。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to start off and set a little context for our listeners, can you give us a 55-second background on some of the wonderful things you've done in your career and what you're up to now?
turns.zh: 首先，请您为我们的听众介绍一些背景信息，您能否用 55 秒的时间向我们介绍一下您在职业生涯中所做的一些精彩的事情以及您现在所做的事情？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Definitely. So I've spent pretty much my entire career in B2B SaaS tech, building and scaling through hyper growth, oftentimes with disruptive technologies at the center of people, tech, future of work. I would say I helped bring products like CultureAmp and Greenhouse to market in the people space. Before that, I did some work in enterprise social networking in the Yammer days. And most recently, I was the CMO at Miro where I also led the rebrand and introduced that product to the world, which was very exciting.
turns.zh: 确实。因此，我的整个职业生涯几乎都花在了 B2B SaaS 技术上，通过超速增长进行构建和扩展，通常以人员、技术和未来工作为中心的颠覆性技术。我想说，我帮助将 CultureAmp 和 Greenhouse 等产品推向了人员领域的市场。在此之前，我在 Yammer 时代做过一些企业社交网络方面的工作。最近，我担任 Miro 的首席营销官，在那里我还领导了品牌重塑并向世界介绍了该产品，这非常令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you've got a startup now, so maybe you just mention that briefly and then we'll talk about it at the end again. Yeah. What are you working on now?
turns.zh: 现在你已经有了一家初创公司，所以也许你只是简单地提到这一点，然后我们会在最后再讨论它。是的。你现在在做什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah. And now, I'm building a product which we'll see about the category what it ends up being, but it's what we call an employee progression platform. So basically, from the work that I've done as a leader, building and scaling teams and also the exposure I've had in the people tech space, I just have found that there's been a lot of tools lacking for leaders to really coach and develop their team in the right way, creating enough structure and transparency into the process that creates accountability on both sides. So yeah, we're taking on the big goal of killing performance reviews.
turns.zh: 是的。现在，我正在构建一个产品，我们将了解它最终的类别，但这就是我们所说的员工进步平台。所以基本上，从我作为领导者所做的工作、建立和扩展团队以及我在人员技术领域的接触来看，我发现领导者缺乏很多工具来真正以正确的方式指导和发展他们的团队，为双方建立问责制的流程创建足够的结构和透明度。所以，是的，我们正在实现消灭绩效评估的大目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy moly. Cool.
turns.zh: 圣钼。凉爽的。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Very exciting
turns.zh: 非常令人兴奋

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Performance reviews. Very exciting. It's true. We'll talk about that a bit at the end more. And there's a bunch of stuff I want to dig into. You have such a cool background on so many interesting experiences. The first is something that you mentioned just now, which is category and category creation, which I know is near and dear to your heart. I was reading a bit about your background, and I learned that at Miro, you invented this category that's now called visual collaboration. And at CultureAmp, I think you helped lead the creation of this category, employee experience. I imagine at Greenhouse, you did something similar. And I know startups are often trying to decide, should I create my own category? Should I try to win in an existing category? And so I want to spend some time talking through your experience there.
turns.zh: 绩效评估。非常令人兴奋。这是真的。我们将在最后进一步讨论这一点。还有很多我想深入研究的东西。你的背景很酷，有很多有趣的经历。第一个是你刚才提到的，就是品类和品类的创造，我知道你很关心这个问题。我读了一些关于你的背景，我了解到，在 Miro，你发明了现在称为视觉协作的类别。在 CultureAmp，我认为您帮助领导了员工体验这一类别的创建。我想你在 Greenhouse 也做了类似的事情。我知道初创公司经常试图决定，我应该创建自己的类别吗？我应该尝试在现有类别中获胜吗？所以我想花一些时间谈谈你在那里的经历。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so the first question is just say at Miro or Greenhouse, can you just talk through your thought process of trying to decide, should we invent a whole new category that we're going to win or should we just try to win an existing category and how did that go?
turns.zh: 所以第一个问题就是在 Miro 或 Greenhouse 说，你能谈谈你试图决定的思考过程吗？我们应该发明一个我们将赢得的全新类别，还是应该尝试赢得一个现有的类别，结果如何？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: They're both great examples because in one, we did create a new category and in the other, we tried and abandoned ship. With Miro, I think when I joined the company, there was this concept of an online whiteboard, which also is a category, but it's a much smaller category and it wasn't something that a lot of people searched for. And I think the biggest motivating factor of thinking about category creation at Miro was how do we become something really big and needed by every company and not just this little thing that maybe product teams would use or maybe engineering teams or schools or something like that.
turns.zh: 它们都是很好的例子，因为在一个中，我们确实创建了一个新类别，而在另一个中，我们尝试并放弃了船舶。对于 Miro，我想当我加入公司时，就有了在线白板的概念，这也是一个类别，但它是一个小得多的类别，而且不是很多人搜索的东西。我认为，在 Miro 思考品类创建的最大推动因素是，我们如何成为真正大的、每个公司都需要的东西，而不仅仅是产品团队、工程团队、学校或类似的东西会使用的小东西。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: When you're thinking about category creation, it's really, for us, it was really about the scope of what we're trying to do and not wanting to be in something too small. And I think with Miro, the platform that it is, there is so much possibility. I used to joke that it was, even as a company, we were the ever expanding universe. There's just so much to do there, but online whiteboard was really small.
turns.zh: 当你考虑品类创建时，对我们来说，这实际上是关于我们正在尝试做的事情的范围，而不是想做太小的事情。我认为，有了 Miro 这个平台，就有很多可能性。我曾经开玩笑说，即使作为一家公司，我们也是不断扩张的宇宙。那里有很多事情要做，但在线白板真的很小。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Greenhouse is in the ATS category, which is applicant tracking system. And at the time, applicant tracking systems had a really bad name. I don't know if folks that listen to this know of Jobvite or remember Jobvite, and there were a lot of systems before that. Jobvite had come in the mid-2000s as the new and improved ATS and it was all about social recruiting, but it was very transactional and it wasn't very strategic. And so we wanted to steer clear of the ATS space even though we were an ATS. We can talk more about what we tried and what we ended up doing, but I think the main factors when you're thinking about category creation is really what budget companies have, if they have a budget, if they don't have a budget. Companies did have a budget for ATS, for example. Until now, I don't think companies had a budget for visual collaboration. For example, what's the language and the words that people use to describe their pain points and their situation, the things that they need? And then is their competition?
turns.zh: Greenhouse 属于 ATS 类别，即申请人跟踪系统。当时，申请人跟踪系统的名声非常不好。我不知道听这个的人是否知道Jobvite或者还记得Jobvite，在这之前已经有很多系统了。 Jobvite 于 2000 年代中期出现，作为新的和改进的 ATS，它完全是关于社会招聘，但它是非常交易性的，并且不是很有战略性。因此，即使我们是 ATS，我们也想避开 ATS 领域。我们可以更多地谈论我们尝试过的事情以及我们最终做了什么，但我认为当你考虑类别创建时，主要因素实际上是预算公司拥有的东西，如果他们有预算，如果他们没有预算。例如，公司确实有 ATS 预算。到目前为止，我认为公司还没有视觉协作的预算。例如，人们用什么语言和词语来描述他们的痛点和他们的情况，他们需要什么？那么他们的竞争是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: And sometimes, competition, you would think like, "Oh, we want to not have competition, so let's build a new category." But ultimately, you're not building a category until there is competition. It's not officially actually a category until there's more companies that do that. And that was a big learning for me in this whole process of category creation, is that it's actually okay when new companies come in that say they're that category because it's just validating the fact that there is a new category. So I think it's really ... If and when is really about what the overall objective is and also what the current situation is with competitors and the space. The ATS market is still the ATS market, for example, and Miro has created visual collaboration as a category but also ticks off boxes for other categories as well.
turns.zh: 有时，竞争，你会想，“哦，我们不想有竞争，所以让我们建立一个新的类别。”但归根结底，在竞争出现之前你不会建立一个类别。在有更多公司这样做之前，它实际上并不是一个正式的类别。在品类创建的整个过程中，这对我来说是一个很大的学习，那就是当新公司进来时说他们是那个品类实际上是可以的，因为这只是验证了存在一个新品类的事实。所以我认为这真的是……是否以及何时真正涉及总体目标是什么以及竞争对手和空间的当前状况。例如，ATS 市场仍然是 ATS 市场，Miro 创建了视觉协作作为一个类别，但也为其他类别打勾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a thousand questions I want to ask to dig deeper. Before we get in there, can you just define, well, what is a category? Folks that are just like, what the hell have you been talking about? What is a product category? What's the high level way to think about this?
turns.zh: 我有一千个问题想问得更深入。在我们开始之前，您能先定义一下什么是类别吗？人们就像，你们到底在说什么？什么是产品类别？思考这个问题的高级方法是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: When we talk about category, I think it's really what would be a good way to explore your space and your relevant categories would be to go to G2 Crowd or Software Advice or any of those type of review sites or directory sites and learn about how they've categorized products based on feature sets. And so within each industry, there's going to be a bunch of different types of categories. Those categories are typically products that solve, at least in B2B products, that solve a certain pain point or a set of pain points, and they can be very wide like all in one and big solutions or they can be narrow. There's this all in one versus best in class, for example. And I think that's where the granularity of category comes into play and then how big the market is. Obviously, maps to granularity versus more broad and when are you granular versus when do you go broad? But I think ultimately, it's just a set of features or products that are solving a specific pain point that customers most likely have a budget allocated for.
turns.zh: 当我们谈论类别时，我认为这确实是探索您的空间的好方法，您的相关类别将转到 G2 Crowd 或 Software Advice 或任何此类评论网站或目录网站，并了解他们如何根据功能集对产品进行分类。因此，在每个行业内，都会有许多不同类型的类别。这些类别通常是解决某个痛点或一组痛点的产品，至少在 B2B 产品中是这样，它们可以非常广泛，例如一体化解决方案，也可以很狭窄。例如，这就是全合一与同类最佳的对比。我认为这就是类别的粒度发挥作用的地方，以及市场有多大。显然，映射到粒度与更广泛的关系，什么时候你是细粒度的，什么时候你是广泛的？但我认为最终，它只是解决客户最有可能分配预算的特定痛点的一组功能或产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then the category ends up, the way you use it is it's the way you pitch your product often. It's like the big part of the headline, part of the way you sell it. It's like you come back to this we're the leader in visual collaboration, for example, or that's how it practically ends up being used.
turns.zh: 然后类别就结束了，你使用它的方式就是你经常推销产品的方式。这就像标题的重要部分，也是你推销标题的方式的一部分。举例来说，就像您回到我们是视觉协作领域的领导者一样，或者这就是它实际上最终被使用的方式。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Exactly. It's interesting because I would say that if you're building a category as well, you can sometimes be selling into a category while you're still building the appetite for a different category, which is a nuance, which is all about where's the budget and how do customers describe their pain points?
turns.zh: 确切地。这很有趣，因为我想说，如果你也在建立一个类别，有时你可以在一个类别中销售，而你仍在建立对不同类别的兴趣，这是一个细微差别，这都是关于预算在哪里以及客户如何描述他们的痛点？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me, I was just trying to pitch my podcast in this little dock I'm writing. And initially, I was like, "Oh, it's like a top hundred business podcast." And I'm like, "No, it's the number one product and growth podcast in the world," which is true, but I created my own category. How about that?
turns.zh: 这提醒了我，我只是想在我正在写的这个小码头上推销我的播客。最初，我想，“哦，这就像百强商业播客。”我想，“不，这是世界上排名第一的产品和增长播客”，这是事实，但我创建了自己的类别。怎么样？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 就这样吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was that a good idea?
turns.zh: 这是个好主意吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I think so. The thing is it's like when you talk about ICP for how you're going to sell your product and really build a repeatable sales process to scale that piece of your business. And the more specific the thing is that you're selling initially, obviously you're going to have more relevant users. They're going to spread word of mouth, etc. You could always expand that scope later. The category can also evolve. You mentioned CultureAmp earlier. The category now is people experience. Actually, when I was there, it was more about people analytics platform or people intelligence platform because we were providing a deep set of data that companies didn't have before, but that category has since evolved as their go-to market has changed, as they've added new products to their platform and new features and things like that.
turns.zh: 我想是的。问题是，就像当您谈论 ICP 时，您将如何销售您的产品，并真正构建一个可重复的销售流程来扩展您的业务。更具体的是，您最初进行销售，显然您将拥有更多相关用户。他们会进行口碑传播，等等。以后你可以随时扩大范围。该类别也可以发展。您之前提到过 CultureAmp。现在的类别是人们的体验。实际上，当我在那里时，更多的是关于人员分析平台或人员智能平台，因为我们提供了公司以前没有的一组深层数据，但随着他们的市场走向发生变化，这个类别已经发生了变化，因为他们在平台上添加了新产品和新功能等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make it even more concrete for people, what are other examples of categories that come to mind that are either invented recently or just generally?
turns.zh: 为了让人们更具体地了解一下，人们想到的类别的其他例子有哪些，这些类别要么是最近发明的，要么只是普遍发明的？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: In the early days, I was working on market automation, for example, so Marketo, now HubSpot, fits into that, even though back then, they were more of this inbound marketing platform/category performance management, which is the area of Pando. We've talked a lot about people, products. I think Gainsight did a great job with the customer success platform, so this is a different problem that they were solving within the organization for a group. The customer success team, basically how are they going to make their customers successful?
turns.zh: 例如，早期我从事市场自动化工作，所以 Marketo（现在的 HubSpot）就适合这一领域，尽管当时他们更多的是这种入站营销平台/品类绩效管理，这是 Pando 的领域。我们谈论了很多关于人、产品的话题。我认为 Gainsight 在客户成功平台方面做得很好，所以这是他们在组织内为一个团队解决的另一个问题。客户成功团队，基本上他们将如何使客户成功？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 惊人的。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, customer success. It's a well name.
turns.zh: 是的，客户的成功。这是一个好名字。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. There's many benefits to try to create your own category, right? We're number one. That's one main category. Two is you can lead the charge on understanding or just defining what's important. I imagine there's other benefits maybe you could share, but there's also probably a lot of downsides. You mentioned oftentimes, it doesn't work and it just ends up being a lot of wasted money. Maybe just talk about what are the reasons to pursue trying to create your own category and then some of the reasons you maybe shouldn't.
turns.zh: 好的。尝试创建自己的类别有很多好处，对吧？我们是第一。这是一个主要类别。二是你可以带头理解或定义什么是重要的。我想您也许可以分享其他好处，但也可能有很多缺点。你经常提到，它不起作用，而且最终会浪费很多钱。也许只是谈谈尝试创建自己的类别的原因是什么，然后谈谈您可能不应该这样做的一些原因。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Greenhouse is a great example to talk about a failed approach at creating a category. So I mentioned before the ATS or the applicant tracking system category at the time was just, it carried so much disdain. People had such bad experiences with that whole category of products. No matter what, they weren't strategic. They didn't help people be good at recruiting. It was just a pretty terrible, very transactional experience. And I came in and it was like, "Okay, let's reposition ourselves. We're going to create a new category." We tried several things.
turns.zh: Greenhouse 是一个很好的例子来讨论创建类别的失败方法。所以我之前提到的 ATS 或申请人跟踪系统当时的类别只是，它带有如此多的蔑视。人们对整个类别的产品都有如此糟糕的体验。无论如何，它们都不是战略性的。他们并没有帮助人们擅长招聘。这是一次非常糟糕、非常交易的经历。当我进来时，感觉就像是，“好吧，让我们重新定位自己。我们将创建一个新的类别。”我们尝试了几件事。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: One of the main things that we zeroed in on was recruiting optimization platform, and it was really like we are doing that. We're helping companies really structure the process, identify where they have gaps, where people are falling through the cracks, where they're flying through the process and really tweak and iterate it and improve it. And we spent time getting content out there, talking to press about it, positioning it in this way. And ultimately, at the end of the day, the budget that customers had and the way that customers talked about what we did, no matter what we called it, was applicant tracking.
turns.zh: 我们关注的主要事情之一是招聘优化平台，我们确实正在这样做。我们正在帮助公司真正构建流程，确定他们的差距在哪里，人们在哪里被忽视，他们在流程中飞翔，并真正调整、迭代和改进它。我们花时间发布内容，与媒体谈论它，并以这种方式定位它。最终，归根结底，客户的预算以及客户谈论我们所做的事情的方式（无论我们称之为什么）都是申请人跟踪。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So it didn't really make sense to continue to go against the grain of, no, we're going to be this new thing or we're going to call it this if everybody, even seeing the value and seeing the differentiation of our platform to others, still called it an ATS. We abandoned that process. But I think the main thing that we understood then was instead of spending the time and money to build a new category, we were going to spend the time and money to elevate the value of this category. So rather than changing the category to something else which we could value at whatever it was, we were just going to spend all of our resources to make this whole category much more valuable to the users, to companies. And that really was, along with what CultureAmp was doing at the time in the same space, what set off this whole trajectory of really good, strong people practices and people organizations that were really doing cool stuff on the recruiting side as well as employee engagement.
turns.zh: 因此，继续违背这样的原则是没有意义的：不，我们将成为这个新事物，或者如果每个人，即使看到了我们平台的价值并看到了我们平台与其他平台的差异化，仍然称其为 ATS，我们将称之为 ATS。我们放弃了这个过程。但我认为我们当时理解的主要事情是，我们不会花时间和金钱来建立一个新的类别，而是要花时间和金钱来提升这个类别的价值。因此，我们不会将类别更改为我们可以重视的其他类别，而只是花费所有资源，使整个类别对用户和公司更有价值。这确实是，连同 CultureAmp 当时在同一领域所做的事情，引发了真正良好、强大的人员实践和人才组织的整个轨迹，这些组织在招聘方面以及员工敬业度方面确实做了很酷的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned a few components of when it makes sense to come up with a category. One is there's budget already against it. Two is people use the words associated with that category. I imagine with Miro and this idea of, what was it, visual collaboration, there wasn't budget for that yet. So how does that work?
turns.zh: 您提到了何时提出一个类别才有意义的一些组成部分。一是已经有预算了。二是人们使用与该类别相关的词语。我想对于米罗和这个视觉协作的想法，目前还没有预算。那么它是如何运作的呢？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: No. That is more of the vision piece, I would say. Sometimes you can have a vision that customers, they don't have it yet or they don't share it, but they can grow to share it and they did in that case. And I think that with Miro, we still worked to optimize where we could in terms of the categories that we did fit into or how people talked about us, but it was also such a new format and it was really a disruptive product that didn't exist before in the enterprise so that it was called a lot of different things. So it was much more fluid and people talked about it in different ways, and this was our way of hearing the feedback about how people talked about it as online whiteboard or lots of jobs to be done were framed, mind mapping platform or diagramming or whatever, all of these little things.
turns.zh: 不，我想说，这更多的是愿景。有时你可以有一个愿景，客户还没有这个愿景，或者他们没有分享它，但他们可以逐渐分享它，在这种情况下他们做到了。我认为，对于 Miro，我们仍然在努力优化我们所适合的类别或人们如何谈论我们，但它也是一种新的格式，它确实是一个颠覆性的产品，以前在企业中不存在，所以它被称为很多不同的东西。所以它更加流畅，人们以不同的方式谈论它，这是我们听到人们如何谈论它的反馈的方式，因为在线白板或许多需要完成的工作被框架，思维导图平台或图表或其他，所有这些小事情。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: And so visual collaboration was our way of putting a nice bow around this thing that could then be an enterprise product that solves a lot of different problems for a lot of different use cases and different types of users. We started out selling and having a lot of users that were in product and in engineering and teams that were used to using whiteboards anyway and then needed to do it in a distributed way, but very quickly packaged different types of jobs for HR teams or marketing teams or design teams and pretty much anybody in the organization. But it needed to all come together cohesively; otherwise, it was like everybody in the org just calls it a different thing because they use it in a different way.
turns.zh: 因此，视觉协作是我们为这个东西打下良好基础的方式，然后它可以成为一个企业产品，为许多不同的用例和不同类型的用户解决许多不同的问题。我们一开始进行销售，并拥有大量产品、工程和团队用户，他们无论如何都习惯使用白板，然后需要以分布式方式进行操作，但很快就为人力资源团队、营销团队或设计团队以及组织中的几乎任何人打包了不同类型的工作。但它需要所有人齐心协力；否则，就好像组织中的每个人都将其称为不同的东西，因为他们以不同的方式使用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Part of what I'm hearing is that you don't stop working on the other categories that it already sits within and just keep optimizing those but in parallel, start to try to pull together, hey, there's this bigger vision of where this could be. Does that sound right?
turns.zh: 我听到的部分内容是，你不会停止对它已经存在的其他类别的工作，只是继续优化它们，但同时，开始尝试整合在一起，嘿，有一个更大的愿景，这可能是。听起来对吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I think so. And it's really where you get the inputs from your customers and your users. We heard all these things. Miro, we did a lot of content marketing. That's a big piece of doing category creation generally I would say. But there's a lot of different ways that people talked about it, and so that's an opportunity to actually come and say, okay, here's what it is because no one knows, and it's all of these things and all of these things together equals this now. And then that created momentum where other companies started thinking like that and then they started tagging themselves as that category as well, and then you had a category of multiple companies now that were doing similar stuff.
turns.zh: 我想是的。这确实是您从客户和用户那里获取输入的地方。我们听到了所有这些事情。米罗，我们做了很多内容营销。我想说，这通常是类别创建的一个重要部分。但人们有很多不同的方式来谈论它，所以这是一个机会来真正说，好吧，这就是它是什么，因为没有人知道，它是所有这些东西，所有这些东西加在一起等于现在。然后这创造了动力，其他公司开始这样思考，然后他们也开始将自己标记为该类别，然后你就有了一个由多家公司组成的类别，它们正在做类似的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. How do you know when it's probably a bad idea to try to create your own category?
turns.zh: 是的，绝对是。你怎么知道什么时候尝试创建自己的类别可能是个坏主意？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: The sooner, the better if you're going to try and fail and iterate. I think if you already are well established, I don't think category creation is really a meaningful effort if you already have ... It's not going to be necessarily a way to just all of a sudden generate new business by creating Q&A new category once you've already gone far enough down the path. I think that if you're not getting ... With the Greenhouse situation, as much as we used this other language and it did get picked up a bit in terms of context that people would use to talk about Greenhouse, it really just wasn't sticking. And so I think it's good to try things and also abandon them and that's okay. You can always sit back into the category. If you really don't fit into any other category, then you probably do need to figure out what the category is and package that. And that's going to be done mostly by continuing to talk to customers and listening to how they talk about things. It all comes from what you hear from them ultimately and what will resonate.
turns.zh: 如果你要尝试失败并迭代，越早越好。我认为，如果你已经很成熟，我不认为类别创建真的是一项有意义的努力，如果你已经……一旦你已经在这条道路上走得足够远，这不一定是通过创建问答新类别突然产生新业务的一种方法。我认为，如果你没有得到……在温室的情况下，尽管我们使用了另一种语言，并且它确实在人们用来谈论温室的上下文中有所体现，但它确实没有坚持下去。所以我认为尝试一些事情并放弃它们是件好事，这没关系。您始终可以回到该类别。如果您确实不适合任何其他类别，那么您可能确实需要弄清楚该类别是什么并将其打包。这主要是通过继续与客户交谈并倾听他们如何谈论事情来完成的。这一切都来自于你最终从他们那里听到的以及会引起共鸣的内容。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So I think, yeah, if you're already established, if you really aren't differentiated from other categories in your space, then you probably are in that category. And doing category creation is a lot of work that is not going to be fruitful if you're pretty squarely in something already. And then if you really aren't but you need to figure it out, you're just going to have to keep iterating until you figure out what makes sense to your customers.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，是的，如果你已经确立了地位，如果你真的没有与你所在领域的其他类别区分开来，那么你可能就属于那个类别。创建类别是一项繁重的工作，如果您已经完全投入某件事，那么这些工作就不会取得成果。然后，如果你确实不是，但你需要弄清楚，你就必须不断迭代，直到弄清楚什么对你的客户有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For founders who are listening to this and they're just like, "Oh, this sounds interesting. I want to try to think about a new category maybe for my product." Can you just talk about the mechanics of going through this process of trying to decide what category it should be called, how to roll it out, anything you could share by just the tactics of creating a category?
turns.zh: 对于听了这个的创始人来说，他们会说，“哦，这听起来很有趣。我想尝试为我的产品考虑一个新的类别。”您能否谈谈尝试决定应将其命名为哪个类别、如何推出它以及您可以通过创建类别的策略来分享的任何内容的过程的机制？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: The main thing which we've talked a little bit about already is really understanding your customers and their pain points and how they talk about things. All of my best marketing and positioning literally comes from having a million conversations with customers and listening to how they solve problems and how our system helps them solve problems and what they're doing and how they talk about stuff. I think that's step one, is really understanding who those buyers are, how they talk about the product, what's the unique differentiator and selling points?
turns.zh: 我们已经讨论过的主要内容是真正了解您的客户及其痛点以及他们如何谈论事物。我所有最好的营销和定位实际上都来自与客户进行一百万次对话，聆听他们如何解决问题以及我们的系统如何帮助他们解决问题以及他们在做什么以及他们如何谈论事情。我认为第一步是真正了解这些买家是谁，他们如何谈论产品，独特的差异化因素和卖点是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: One thing that's really important in category creation as well is actually PR. You need to get this category and positioning out there at a high level in order to test it out and see if it makes sense and if it's resonating. And then the other piece is really those directory sites, which the analysts like Gartner and Forrester and all these guys, at least in B2B and enterprise, they really shape for customers what the categories are. And you need to build relationships with them. You need to work with them to create your category as well. So with the visual collaboration, for example, we weren't ranking, we weren't categorized in visual collaboration on G2 Crowd, and we had to meet with them and explain what it was and talk to them about the differentiation of this category versus other categories in terms of features and all of that stuff so that they could understand how they would differentiate this category from another category.
turns.zh: 在类别创建中真正重要的一件事实际上是公关。你需要获得这个类别并在高水平上进行定位，以便对其进行测试，看看它是否有意义以及是否能引起共鸣。另一个部分实际上是那些目录网站，像 Gartner 和 Forrester 这样的分析师以及所有这些人，至少在 B2B 和企业领域，他们真正为客户塑造了类别。你需要与他们建立关系。您还需要与他们合作来创建您的类别。例如，在视觉协作方面，我们没有排名，没有被归入 G2 Crowd 上的视觉协作类别，我们必须与他们会面并解释它是什么，并与他们讨论该类别与其他类别在功能和所有方面的区别，以便他们能够了解如何将该类别与其他类别区分开来。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So I think those are really good channels to look at. And then tactically, it's a lot of content marketing and a lot of thought leadership. When you're building a category, you need to make sure that there is a category that's validated by analysts and directory sites and things like that. But also, you want to have a lot of traction in terms of thought leadership like why is this the category? What are the unique value propositions of this particular thing? What are the pain points it solves? And then of course, getting a lot of content around because when you're generating a new category, you're also needing to educate buyers that there is a category that they can now budget for and why they should allocate budget for that.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这些都是非常值得关注的渠道。然后在战术上，这是大量的内容营销和大量的思想领导力。当您构建类别时，您需要确保有一个类别经过分析师和目录网站等的验证。而且，你希望在思想领导力方面有很大的吸引力，比如为什么是这个类别？这个特定事物的独特价值主张是什么？它解决了哪些痛点？当然，要获得大量内容，因为当你生成一个新类别时，你还需要教育买家，他们现在可以为某个类别进行预算，以及为什么他们应该为此分配预算。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like a hell of a lot of work.
turns.zh: 听起来工作量很大。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: It's a lot.
turns.zh: 很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious. What percentage of say B2B companies do you think should pursue creating a category? Is it almost none or is it a meaningful percentage?
turns.zh: 我很好奇。您认为有多少比例的 B2B 公司应该追求创建一个品类？是几乎没有还是一个有意义的百分比？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: It goes in waves with the tech innovations. So for example, when there was the whole first web wave and then there was this whole social enterprise and consumerization of IT was a big change in how technology occurred in the workplace and a lot of new categories came at that point. So I feel like it's less about the raw percentage and more about general inflection points that are happening that are causing the need for this.
turns.zh: 它随着技术创新的浪潮而发展。例如，当出现第一次网络浪潮，然后出现整个社会企业和 IT 消费化时，技术在工作场所的发生方式发生了巨大变化，许多新类别在那时出现。因此，我觉得这与原始百分比无关，而更多与正在发生的一般拐点有关，这些拐点导致了这种需要。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: And I take COVID for example and this very quick shift to distributed work was one of those type of inflection points that has changed a lot. A new category that has grown extremely fast is, and I don't even know exactly what they call it, but it's these employment platforms like Deel and Oyster that have cropped up and grown significantly fast and also have created a new category where there was already the ability to hire people in all of these distributed places, but you had to find a company in that place that would then hire the people. And then of course, they created these platforms where, hey, here's a system, you can manage it all here, we'll go and build all those relationships on the ground. And Nayya is a new set of a new category with four or five companies just in the last three years that have cropped up. So I think it's more about what the market demands and what's happening in the market rather than whether or not one company it makes sense for, if that makes sense.
turns.zh: 我以新冠疫情为例，这种向分布式工作的快速转变是发生了很大变化的拐点之一。一个增长非常快的新类别是，我什至不知道他们到底叫它什么，但像 Deel 和 Oyster 这样的就业平台突然出现并增长得非常快，并且还创建了一个新类别，已经有能力在所有这些分散的地方雇用人员，但你必须在那个地方找到一家可以雇用人员的公司。当然，他们创建了这些平台，嘿，这是一个系统，你可以在这里管理一切，我们将在实地建立所有这些关系。 Nayya 是一个新类别的新集合，仅在过去三年中就出现了四五家公司。因此，我认为更多的是市场需求和市场正在发生的事情，而不是它对一家公司是否有意义（如果有意义的话）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, makes sense. It depends on where the tide is pulling everyone. I think that makes a lot of sense.
turns.zh: 是的，有道理。这取决于潮流将每个人拉向何处。我认为这很有道理。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 确切地。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one last question about category creation. So on the surface, there's this binary choice. Either try to become the best ATS platform or we're not ATS, we're employee recruiting automation. Is there a middle ground? Do you have to go one or the other or is there some in between route, maybe positioning a little bit differently or how do you think about that?
turns.zh: 也许是关于类别创建的最后一个问题。所以从表面上看，存在这种二元选择。要么努力成为最好的 ATS 平台，要么我们就不是 ATS，我们是员工招聘自动化。有中间立场吗？您是否必须选择其中之一，或者中间是否有一些路线，也许定位略有不同，或者您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: There could be some middle ground. I would say for Pando, for example, performance management is a very established category that we technically fit into, and also there's a line item on the budget and people have money to pay for performance management. But we're introducing this concept of employee progression, which is more of a long tail strategy. So while we want to educate the market and build this new category of employee progression because it's related to the differences between what we're doing and traditional performance management, we're still going to rate ourselves in directory sites, for example, or categorize ourselves as performance management and talk about performance management and sell to companies that are looking for performance management. But ultimately, we want to shift everybody's mindset and change the category.
turns.zh: 可能有一些中间立场。例如，我想说，对于 Pando，绩效管理是一个非常成熟的类别，我们在技术上适合它，而且预算中有一个项目，人们有钱支付绩效管理费用。但我们正在引入员工晋升的概念，这更像是一种长尾策略。因此，虽然我们希望教育市场并建立这种新的员工晋升类别，因为它与我们正在做的事情和传统绩效管理之间的差异有关，但我们仍然会在目录网站中对自己进行评级，例如，或者将自己归类为绩效管理并谈论绩效管理并向正在寻求绩效管理的公司推销。但最终，我们希望改变每个人的思维方式并改变类别。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So it's not necessarily one or the other, but I do think the investment is high if you want to build a new category, and we're committed to an investment of time and thought leadership and content and all of that stuff, but it's also not our strategy right now to go and create employee progression and own and dominate this. We're going to work our way up to that over time.
turns.zh: 所以这不一定是其中之一，但我确实认为，如果你想建立一个新的类别，投资就很高，而且我们致力于时间、思想领导力、内容以及所有这些东西的投资，但现在去创造员工进步、拥有并主导这一点也不是我们的战略。随着时间的推移，我们将努力实现这一目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. That connects to what you talked about with Miro. It wasn't like we're switching, we're now visual collaboration. It's like we're still whiteboards, we're the best white boarding tool, but let's also start building this brand of visual collaboration so that people start to learn.
turns.zh: 知道了。这与你和米罗谈论的事情有关。我们并不是在切换，而是现在进行视觉协作。就像我们仍然是白板一样，我们是最好的白板工具，但我们也开始构建这个视觉协作品牌，以便人们开始学习。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Exactly. And I think it's a bottoms up mentality much like our business model was there because with marketing automation, it wasn't a progressive buildup. It was marketing automation. That's what the category was. I was working for a company that was doing marketing automation. There was Eloqua and Marketo and several others and we all were just telling everybody, educating the market on what that was, and that was very top down.
turns.zh: 确切地。我认为这是一种自下而上的心态，就像我们的商业模式一样，因为营销自动化并不是渐进式的积累。这是营销自动化。这就是类别。我在一家从事营销自动化的公司工作。有 Eloqua 和 Marketo 以及其他几个公司，我们只是告诉每个人，让市场了解那是什么，这是非常自上而下的。

turns.zh: 惊人的。本集由 Vanta 为您带来，帮助您简化安全合规性以加速增长。如果您的企业在云中存储任何数据，那么您可能会被询问或将被询问有关 SOC 2 合规性的问题。 SOC 2 是一种证明您的公司正在采取适当的安全措施来保护客户数据并与客户和合作伙伴（尤其是那些有严格安全要求的客户和合作伙伴）建立信任的方法。此外，如果你想向企业销售产品，证明安全性至关重要。 SOC 2 可以为更大、更好的交易打开大门，也可以让您的业务暂停。如果您没有 SOC 2，您很可能甚至无法获得席位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know another area that you spend a lot of time thinking about and you've done a lot of work around is branding, rebranding even and just go to market in general. I know at Miro, you led the charge on rebranding Miro. It used to be called I think RealtimeBoard, the little two capital letters and no space.
turns.zh: 我知道你花了很多时间思考并且做了很多工作的另一个领域是品牌，甚至重塑品牌，然后进入一般市场。我知道在米罗，你带头负责米罗的品牌重塑。我认为它以前被称为 RealtimeBoard，只有两个大写字母，没有空格。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And with Greenhouse, you basically led the go-to market plan. And so I want to spend a little time here I guess just around rebranding. At Miro, it's a rebrand. How do you know it's time to rebrand your product and it's worth investing there?
turns.zh: 通过 Greenhouse，您基本上领导了进入市场计划。所以我想在这里花一点时间，我想只是围绕品牌重塑。对于 Miro，这是一次品牌重塑。您如何知道是时候对您的产品进行品牌重塑并且值得投资？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: RealtimeBoard was interesting. I almost didn't join because it was called RealtimeBoard. Honestly, I was like, "Oh my, god. This is so literal." While I was walking the dogs with my husband, I'm like, "Am I really going to join a company called RealtimeBoard" Can this be a big company with that name?" I was really concerned about it and ultimately, I spent more time with the leaders there and I was like, "Okay, I think they'll be open to changing the name." So I think there's a maturity piece. A lot of companies are started and you just come up with a name and you don't put a lot of thought into it and then you grow to a certain level. At that time, I think we were a million users, maybe a couple of million in revenue so it was very early days. You had a name, you came up with it, you got the website and then the business grew, and at some point, can it be as big as we want it to be, as we think it can be with that name? And I think that was my biggest thing.
turns.zh: RealtimeBoard 很有趣。我差点没加入，因为它叫RealtimeBoard。老实说，我当时想，“天哪。这太字面意思了。”当我和丈夫一起遛狗时，我想，“我真的要加入一家名为 RealtimeBoard 的公司吗？这会是一家用这个名字的大公司吗？”我真的很担心，最终，我花了更多时间与那里的领导者相处，我想，“好吧，我认为他们会愿意更改名称。”所以我认为这是一个成熟的部分。很多公司刚成立时，你只是想出了一个名字，而你没有花太多时间思考。然后你成长到一定程度，我认为我们有一百万用户，也许有几百万的收入，所以你有一个名字，你想出了它，你得到了网站，然后业务增长了，在某个时候，它可以像我们想象的那样大吗？我认为这是我最重要的事情。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: With RealtimeBoard specifically, it was so literal and matter of fact and the product itself had so much more potential than the name was doing justice for. So I think at some point, it's common for companies to do a rebrand once they go into scale mode before you have too many people and before you invest too much obviously in building that brand. So I think the sooner, the better like rebrand before I even joined. Will they let me change the name was my criteria for joining. And I would say in general, the sooner, the better, but obviously after you know that you have product market fit and you have something to scale, so you don't want to invest too much in a brand that isn't going to get you as far as you want to get if you're going to obviously scale.
turns.zh: 具体来说，对于 RealtimeBoard，它是如此字面意义和事实，而且产品本身的潜力比其名称所描述的要大得多。因此，我认为在某些时候，公司在进入规模模式后，在拥有太多人员并且在建立品牌方面投入过多之前，进行品牌重塑是很常见的。所以我认为在我加入之前重塑品牌越早越好。他们是否允许我改名是我加入的标准。我想说的是，一般来说，越早越好，但显然在你知道你的产品适合市场并且你有一些东西可以扩展之后，所以你不想在一个品牌上投入太多，如果你要明显扩展的话，它不会让你达到你想要的程度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to ask you what it took to convince the founders to rebrand because that's often a big challenge, but it sounds like that's part of your employee agreement. I will join if you give me the right to explore this.
turns.zh: 我本来想问你如何说服创始人重塑品牌，因为这通常是一个巨大的挑战，但听起来这是你员工协议的一部分。如果你给我探索这个的权利，我就会加入。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: They were pretty receptive to it. The company was not US-based. I had spent my whole career in Silicon Valley a lot of time with brand and inbound and community-focused brands. So they were pretty receptive. It was not that hard to convince them, which was great. I think the scary part for them and many people was just there was some equity. They did have advocates like how would this impact the people who really loved the product right now? And so one of the things that was really important as we transitioned was that we kept as much of the essence of the initial brand. Before, the logo was like a Post-it and then RealtimeBoard. And so that Post-it, for example, that yellow became the new M that we used, and we actually proposed a hot pink M initially and the yellow M was the, okay, we don't want to go too far from the RealtimeBoard with the yellow Post-it and this was a way to nob to the early base of customers and keep something that was pretty standard and pretty core to the initial brand and name.
turns.zh: 他们对此非常乐于接受。该公司并非总部位于美国。我的整个职业生涯都在硅谷度过，很多时间都花在品牌、入境品牌和以社区为中心的品牌上。所以他们很容易接受。说服他们并不难，这很棒。我认为对他们和许多人来说，可怕的是存在一些公平性。他们确实有拥护者，比如这会对现在真正喜欢该产品的人产生什么影响？因此，在我们转型过程中，真正重要的事情之一就是我们尽可能多地保留了最初品牌的精髓。之前，徽标就像便利贴，然后是 RealtimeBoard。例如，黄色便利贴就成了我们使用的新 M，我们实际上最初提出了亮粉色 M，黄色 M 是，好吧，我们不想用黄色便利贴与 RealtimeBoard 走得太远，这是一种吸引早期客户群的方式，并保留一些非常标准且非常核心的初始品牌和名称。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Looking back, do you think that was worth the effort and time to worry about those folks?
turns.zh: 回想起来，您认为值得花费精力和时间来担心这些人吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay.
turns.zh: 是的。好的。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Oh, the early folk, we definitely got feedback from along the way. We did case studies throughout the process. We got feedback on logos. We got feedback on brand and designs, and there were plenty of people who were like, "Oh, I like RealtimeBoard. It's straightforward." They loved their product, but ultimately, we kept many of them informed and we really involved them in the process to the degree of not slowing us down but still getting feedback, because we did all of this in a very short period of time on top of it. And I think it was worth it because they felt really good about the outcome as well.
turns.zh: 哦，早期的人们，我们一路上肯定得到了反馈。我们在整个过程中进行了案例研究。我们收到了有关徽标的反馈。我们收到了有关品牌和设计的反馈，很多人都说，“哦，我喜欢 RealtimeBoard。它很简单。”他们喜欢他们的产品，但最终，我们让他们中的许多人了解情况，我们真正让他们参与到这个过程中，既不拖慢我们的速度，又仍然得到反馈，因为我们在很短的时间内完成了所有这些工作。我认为这是值得的，因为他们对结果也感觉很好。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: And a big part of rebranding also means that you have to bring the whole company along too and make sure they feel really good about the outcome. And that was probably one of my big takeaways, is just at that time, we were already about a hundred people, so it wasn't a super small company, and everybody had thoughts and feelings and the company had been around for quite a long time before that. So it was a big change for many people.
turns.zh: 品牌重塑的一个重要部分还意味着你必须让整个公司也参与进来，并确保他们对结果感到非常满意。这可能是我最大的收获之一，就在那时，我们已经有大约一百人，所以这不是一家超级小公司，每个人都有想法和感受，而且公司在那之前已经存在了很长一段时间。所以这对很多人来说都是一个很大的改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other learnings from that experience about just going through a branding or rebranding? Maybe just focusing on rebranding. Any other learnings for future rebranding efforts?
turns.zh: 从这次经历中学到的关于品牌塑造或品牌重塑的其他经验教训吗？也许只是专注于品牌重塑。对于未来的品牌重塑工作还有其他学习经验吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So rebranding is just the visual aesthetic, and I think that's important to make sure you can transition in a way that you're still nodding to the original things but you've reinvented it or transformed it in a way that makes more sense for where you're at and where you're going. If you're changing the name, it's way more complicated because everybody has to be involved, legal, all the contracts, the website, the product, all the links. We changed our URL. Everything changed. And so I think it's really important that you have to mobilize and align and have a very clear vision about the process and the steps and be very transparent about it. I think a lot of times, marketing teams just go and do their thing and come back and it's like, "Here we go."
turns.zh: 因此，品牌重塑只是视觉美学，​​我认为重要的是要确保你能够以一种仍然对原始事物点头的方式进行过渡，但你已经重新发明它或以一种对你所处的位置和你要去的地方更有意义的方式改变它。如果你要更改名称，事情会变得更加复杂，因为每个人都必须参与，法律，所有合同，网站，产品，所有链接。我们更改了网址。一切都变了。因此，我认为非常重要的是，您必须动员起来并进行协调，并对流程和步骤有非常清晰的愿景，并且对此非常透明。我想很多时候，营销团队只是去做他们的事情，然后回来就像，“我们开始了。”

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: With the rebrand at Miro, it was very much rebrand as a product approach. It was very much a product development process with sprint teams and agile, coming back, and you had owners for different parts of things and all reporting back and it really required everybody in some way to be involved. As I mentioned, we did it in a very condensed period of time. I think we kicked off the naming process in end of October and we launched publicly at South by Southwest with a fully three dimensional booth in March. So it was very short to get a name, and then once we had the name, to do all the actual brand and then not only that but produce an entire booth and event collateral and all of that stuff. So I think mobilizing, having a really strong clear process and delegating and letting go in the marketing role, not trying to own everything. It has to be owned by everybody else because you need sales decks and it's just everything.
turns.zh: 随着 Miro 的品牌重塑，它在很大程度上是一种产品方法的重塑。这在很大程度上是一个由冲刺团队和敏捷回来的产品开发过程，并且你有不同部分的所有者和所有报告，这确实需要每个人以某种方式参与。正如我提到的，我们是在非常紧凑的时间内完成的。我想我们在 10 月底就开始了命名过程，并在 3 月份在西南偏南大会上公开推出了一个完全三维的展位。因此，获得一个名称的时间非常短，一旦我们有了名称，就可以做所有实际的品牌，然后不仅如此，还制作整个展位和活动宣传品以及所有这些东西。因此，我认为要动员起来，制定一个非常强大、清晰的流程，并委派和放弃营销角色，而不是试图拥有一切。它必须为其他人所拥有，因为你需要销售平台，而它就是一切。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I think there's also luck involved with any success and also in rebrands because a million things could go wrong. We got our domain name changed to miro.com, I think it was 48 hours before the event.
turns.zh: 我认为任何成功和品牌重塑都需要运气，因为一百万件事都可能出错。我们的域名已更改为 miro.com，我想是在活动前 48 小时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh damn.
turns.zh: 哦该死。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: All the material had been printed with the new URL. We had to just make a leap of faith, super stressful, but thankfully, we had luck on our side. But ultimately, team process, clear structure, transparent for everybody, getting feedback from customers and making sure stakeholders feel like they're involved. I think ultimately, it's a really powerful way to create defensibility for a product and a brand in the market, but it's also a lot of work related to category creation.
turns.zh: 所有材料都已印有新的 URL。我们必须实现信念的飞跃，压力很大，但幸运的是，我们有运气。但最终，团队流程、清晰的结构、对每个人都透明、从客户那里获得反馈并确保利益相关者感觉他们参与其中。我认为最终，这是为产品和品牌在市场上创造防御力的一种非常有效的方式，但它也需要做很多与品类创建相关的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just going to say that. It sounds like everything you do is just a hell of a lot of work. The rest [inaudible 00:37:34].
turns.zh: 我正要这么说。听起来你所做的一切都只是大量的工作。其余的 [听不清 00:37:34]。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: It's fun. I love work.
turns.zh: 很有趣。我热爱工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Me too. I always joke that I work for a workaholic, which is myself.
turns.zh: 我也是。我总是开玩笑说我是在为一个工作狂工作，也就是我自己。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah, I do. I know. I just love it. So I get into this stuff and I think rebranding and category creation and brand in general, I think what our goal with Miro was to create ... There's this concept of a love mark rather than a straight mark. It's like how do you build a brand? I think Airbnb has done a great job with that as well, but how do you build a brand that people really love and so committed to and invested in? And that you have to put a lot of thought into it, and it needs to be authentic for it to really work, but if it does, it's super, super powerful.
turns.zh: 是的，我愿意。我知道。我就是喜欢它。所以我开始研究这个东西，我认为品牌重塑、品类创建和品牌总体而言，我认为我们与米罗的目标是创造……有一个爱标记而不是直标记的概念。就像你如何建立一个品牌？我认为 Airbnb 在这方面也做得很好，但如何打造一个人们真正喜爱、忠诚并投资的品牌呢？你必须花很多心思，它必须是真实的才能真正发挥作用，但如果它确实有效，那么它就非常非常强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I was there during the Airbnb rebrand. It took I think a year and a half for them from start to finish to get to something they were really excited about ready to launch. And there's also actually a similar story to the domain story shared with the font. I don't know how much I could share, but they didn't have the right to use the font until the last day or something. It was a close call.
turns.zh: 是的。 Airbnb 品牌重塑期间我就在场。我认为他们从开始到完成花了一年半的时间才完成了他们真正兴奋的准备推出的事情。实际上还有一个与字体共享的领域故事类似的故事。我不知道我能分享多少，但直到最后一天或其他时间他们才有权使用该字体。这是一次千钧一发的机会。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah, but you have to just like, "It's going to happen." There's some blind faith.
turns.zh: 是的，但你必须喜欢“这将会发生”。有一些盲目的信仰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. It helps close it. We're launching. I wanted to talk about just branding in general. You've worked on such great, big, successful brands and you've helped craft these brands, and I'm just curious what advice you have around just building a brand, a lasting brand, a global brand. What's important when you think about creating a brand for your startup?
turns.zh: 正确的。它有助于关闭它。我们要发射了我想谈谈一般的品牌建设。你曾为如此伟大、大、成功的品牌工作过，并且帮助打造了这些品牌，我只是好奇你对建立一个品牌、一个持久的品牌、一个全球品牌有什么建议。当您考虑为您的初创公司创建品牌时，什么最重要？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I think it's something that companies should think about as early as possible and have it not be an afterthought. The product and the brand are the main things that will get customers and keep them and also keep them loyal and engaged. So I think you have to have both. You can't have one or the other. You could have a great brand and if the product sucks, there's only so far a brand can go. And you also can have a great product and maybe not that thoughtful of a brand, but what I've found is that the more the brand is interchangeable with the people at the company and the company itself, the stronger it is, the more authentic it is. When you talk about Google, you also talk about its people. They're one and the same Googlers. And a lot of companies have that same approach.
turns.zh: 我认为这是企业应该尽早考虑的事情，而不是事后才想到的。产品和品牌是吸引客户、留住客户、保持忠诚度和参与度的主要因素。所以我认为你必须两者兼得。你不能同时拥有其中之一。你可以拥有一个伟大的品牌，但如果产品很糟糕，那么这个品牌就只能走这么远了。你也可以拥有一个很棒的产品，也许不是一个经过深思熟虑的品牌，但我发现，品牌与公司人员和公司本身的互换性越强，它就越强大，就越真实。当你谈论谷歌时，你也在谈论它的员工。他们是同一位 Google 员工。许多公司也采取同样的方法。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: And I think with Miro, we definitely incorporate our values into the brand. Our whole mission was to help companies build the next big thing. This is what we want to do. We want to be the platform that helps companies build the next big thing. We also had to be a big thing. We need to show what big things are. And so your company values, for example, can shape how big and how deep you go with your brand, how authentic it is to the experiences that people have because ultimately, values play a big part because values are foundational to how people behave at the organization, how they work together, how they work with one another, how they work with customers, how they talk to customers.
turns.zh: 我认为通过 Miro，我们肯定会将我们的价值观融入到品牌中。我们的整个使命是帮助公司打造下一个伟大的事物。这就是我们想做的。我们希望成为帮助公司打造下一个伟大事物的平台。我们还必须成为一件大事。我们需要展示什么是大事。例如，你的公司价值观可以决定你的品牌有多大、有多深，以及人们的体验有多真实，因为归根结底，价值观起着重要作用，因为价值观是人们在组织中的行为方式、他们如何一起工作、他们如何彼此合作、他们如何与客户合作以及他们如何与客户交谈的基础。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: The best way to incorporate your brand and how people are interacting with people that you are selling to, customers or whoever, partners, is to have those values incorporated because then it's every touchpoint isn't something that you have to train people, okay, these are all the touch points and this is how the brand needs to manifest. It already will because it's part of the DNA of the company. So I think really integrating the values can help with that and also, of course, make the brand itself human and authentic and something that people really feel emotional connection to.
turns.zh: 整合你的品牌以及人们如何与你的销售对象、客户或任何人、合作伙伴互动的最佳方式就是整合这些价值观，因为这样你就不需要对每个接触点进行培训，好吧，这些都是接触点，这就是品牌需要体现的方式。它已经会了，因为它是公司 DNA 的一部分。因此，我认为真正整合价值观可以对此有所帮助，当然，也可以使品牌本身变得人性化和真实，并且使人们真正感受到情感联系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of value informing the brand or change or helping you make a different decision maybe at Miro or CultureAmp or Greenhouse to make that a little more concrete?
turns.zh: 有什么价值的例子可以告诉品牌或改变，或者帮助你在 Miro、CultureAmp 或 Greenhouse 做出不同的决定，使之更具体一些？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Authenticity as a value. Candor as a value. Thoughtfulness as a value. If you have a value around a bias for action or something like that, these things can translate to how the brand manifests in terms of the language that's used, the colors, the objects. With Miro, for example, we had each character of the word Miro in a different shape, and each shape had different characteristics and those were tied back to different values so they each represented something different.
turns.zh: 真实性作为一种价值。坦率作为一种价值观。体贴作为一种价值观。如果你有一个关于行动偏见或类似的价值观，这些东西可以转化为品牌如何在所使用的语言、颜色和物体方面体现出来。例如，对于“米罗”，我们将“米罗”这个词的每个字符都有不同的形状，每个形状都有不同的特征，而这些特征又与不同的值相关联，因此它们各自代表不同的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of that? What were Miro's values while we're diving into there?
turns.zh: 有什么例子吗？当我们深入探讨时，米罗的价值观是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: One of them was around agility. And so, one, I don't remember which letter it was. Maybe the I. It was shaped wiggly, and then we also had a visual manifestation of it so they all behaved differently. They all had their own behavior. And one of the things that was really important to us is that we were creating a visual system or a visual language so that people that were from different parts of the world, working together could understand each other without necessarily speaking the same language. And so this was a way to invoke this connection of different perspectives and different languages in a way that got all pulled together.
turns.zh: 其中之一是敏捷性。所以，第一，我不记得那是哪封信了。也许是 I。它的形状是摆动的，然后我们也有它的视觉表现，所以它们的行为都不同。他们都有自己的行为。对我们来说真正重要的事情之一是，我们正在创建一个视觉系统或视觉语言，以便来自世界不同地区的人们一起工作可以互相理解，而不必说同一种语言。因此，这是一种以一种将不同观点和不同语言结合在一起的方式来调用这种联系的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Cool. There's a lot there. The way you all visualized the values were using the name Miro. I imagine there's four values then.
turns.zh: 知道了。凉爽的。那里有很多东西。你们所有的可视化值的方式都是使用米罗这个名字。我想有四个值。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then Agility as a value informed the product. It needs to be agile and make sure people can be flexible in how they use it.
turns.zh: 然后敏捷性作为一种价值体现在产品中。它需要敏捷并确保人们可以灵活地使用它。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Definitely. How we build the product, how people around the product act, and then that shape itself was agile and moved and agiley.
turns.zh: 确实。我们如何构建产品，产品周围的人们如何行动，然后这个形状本身是敏捷的、移动的和敏捷的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. I love that. Were you there for coming up with the values? People are always wondering, just how do we come up with our company values? Do you have any insights into just developing company values?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我喜欢那个。你是为了提出这些价值观而存在的吗？人们总是想知道，我们如何制定公司价值观？您对发展公司价值观有什么见解吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: We did iterations of it while I was there. They already had a stake in the ground. What I have done in the past with values is we just did an exercise with my leadership team, for example, where we did a workshop format. We actually used Miro where everybody just brain dumped their ideas around values, and then it was, okay, from there, let's group them into themes. And then from there, let's vote on the most important things. And then from there, how do we start to articulate and define these things? Ultimately, coming up with the definitions is not really something you can do as a group because it's just not very productive. It's better if somebody who knows how to write well can come up with the first stab of the sentences, if it's operating principles, if it's values, and then get feedback on it. But you can get everybody's input and make the process pretty structured by doing something like that where it's like brain dump, group, vote, and then you have your short list of things that you can then work to define.
turns.zh: 当我在那里时，我们对其进行了迭代。他们已经在地上占有了股份。我过去在价值观方面所做的只是与我的领导团队一起进行了一次练习，例如，我们举办了研讨会。我们实际上使用了 Miro，每个人都只是围绕价值观倾倒他们的想法，然后，好吧，从那里开始，让我们将它们分组为主题。然后，让我们对最重要的事情进行投票。然后从那里开始，我们如何开始阐明和定义这些东西？最终，提出定义并不是真正可以作为一个团队完成的事情，因为它的效率不高。如果一个懂得如何写得好的人能够提出句子的第一句话，如果它是操作原则，如果它是价值观，然后获得反馈，那就更好了。但是你可以得到每个人的意见，通过做一些类似的事情，比如头脑风暴、分组、投票，让这个过程变得相当结构化，然后你就得到了你可以定义的简短的事情清单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Maybe one last question around brand. People that aren't in, say, marketing hear brand and it's, okay, it's this fuzzy thing that I feel about our company. When you think about creating a brand, what are the bullet point things that you come up with? There's a logo. There's color palette. Can you just talk through, what is a brand when you're creating a brand and building a brand, what are the elements of it?
turns.zh: 惊人的。也许是关于品牌的最后一个问题。不从事营销工作的人听到品牌时，好吧，我对我们公司的感觉就是这种模糊的东西。当您考虑创建一个品牌时，您想到的要点是什么？有一个标志。有调色板。您能不能讲一下，在创建品牌、打造品牌的时候，什么是品牌，它的要素是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So all of those things that you mentioned. I would say the logo, the colors, the fonts, all the general aesthetic. Do you have photography? Do you use illustrations? Is it all illustrations, all graphics, whatever? You decide those things. You need to understand what the voice is of the brand, how the brand sounds when you write things, when you market it, how people talk. All of that stuff is part of the brand. If you want to build a brand that's really scalable, you think about it more as a system like a brand system. So this is creating things that ... With Miro, for example, we had the letters and we had the colors and we had these concepts of agility. I don't remember all of them off the top of my head, but all of these different concepts that then were represented by different shapes or different colors that could be used in various forms. So it's really like how does it become an extension of all of the different things that you're going to be doing visually or when you talk to customers or how you present the product, etc.?
turns.zh: 所以你提到的所有这些事情。我想说的是标志、颜色、字体，所有一般的审美。你有摄影吗？你使用插图吗？都是插图、图形还是什么？这些事情由你决定。你需要了解品牌的声音是什么，当你写东西时，当你营销它时，品牌听起来如何，人们如何谈论。所有这些东西都是品牌的一部分。如果你想建立一个真正可扩展的品牌，你可以将其更多地视为一个像品牌系统这样的系统。所以这正在创造一些东西......例如，对于米罗，我们有字母，我们有颜色，我们有这些敏捷的概念。我记不起所有这些，但所有这些不同的概念都由不同的形状或不同的颜色代表，可以以各种形式使用。所以这真的就像它如何成为你将要在视觉上做的所有不同事情的延伸，或者当你与客户交谈或如何展示产品等时？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And all of that combines to this feeling you get eventually from the brand. All these things create that fuzzy feeling.
turns.zh: 所有这些结合在一起，最终形成了您从品牌中获得的这种感觉。所有这些都会造成那种模糊的感觉。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's interesting you don't remember all the values at Miro. With Airbnb, I'm just like, I will never forget the Airbnb values. They've been so drilled into our heads.
turns.zh: 是的。有趣的是，你不记得米罗的所有价值观。对于 Airbnb，我永远不会忘记 Airbnb 的价值观。它们已经深深地印在我们的脑海里了。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah, it's because they were too long. It was something that we were constantly working on because they were too long and there were too many things in them to remember. That was the problem.
turns.zh: 是的，就是因为时间太长了。这是我们一直在努力的事情，因为它们太长，而且里面有太多东西需要记住。这就是问题所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great learning there. Make them simple, but also don't make them generic.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的学习。让它们变得简单，但也不要让它们变得通用。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah, it can't be generic, but it also can't be too much that nobody knows what they are. They need to be simple and straightforward and easy to remember.
turns.zh: 是的，它不能太通用，但也不能太通用，以至于没人知道它们是什么。它们需要简单明了且易于记忆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And potentially, illustrated with your company name. That's a really cool idea.
turns.zh: 并可能用您的公司名称进行说明。这真是一个很酷的主意。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 确切地。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last topic I want to spend a little time on is something that I know you're really passionate about, which is this idea of creating opinionated software that has clear opinions about how you should be using it and how you should be doing your work. And so maybe as a first question, just what is opinionated software? What's important about it?
turns.zh: 我想花一点时间讨论的最后一个主题是我知道您真正热衷的事情，即创建固执己见的软件的想法，该软件对您应该如何使用它以及应该如何开展工作有明确的意见。所以也许作为第一个问题，什么是固执己见的软件？这有什么重要的呢？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Opinionated software is basically software platforms that essentially have either best practices or maybe some rules integrated into the system. You have systems that you can customize any which way and however you want and then you have other systems that enforce a certain way of behaving or doing work, as you said. And so I think probably a pretty well known example for your audience especially is Atlassian really building tools for agile workflows and agile teams.
turns.zh: 自以为是的软件基本上是软件平台，本质上要么具有最佳实践，要么集成了一些规则到系统中。正如您所说，您拥有可以以任何方式和方式自定义的系统，然后您还有其他系统强制执行某种行为或工作方式。因此，我认为对于您的观众来说，Atlassian 可能是一个非常知名的例子，它确实为敏捷工作流程和敏捷团队构建了工具。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: And Greenhouse is another example from a recruiting perspective in terms of what we called structured recruiting. There was a very specific way to create a pipeline, build an interview kit, and all of that was important because it made recruiting better and more transparent and obviously less bias and all of those things. So it's principled, I would say. It's anchored in some values. And because of those values, there will be certain rules that are built in that you can't really work around.
turns.zh: 从招聘角度来看，Greenhouse 是我们所谓的结构化招聘的另一个例子。有一种非常具体的方法来创建管道、构建面试工具包，所有这些都很重要，因为它使招聘变得更好、更透明，并且明显减少了偏见等等。所以我想说，这是有原则的。它植根于某些价值观。由于这些价值观，将会存在某些您无法真正解决的内置规则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any advice for when it makes sense to be very opinionated about how you make people use your product and do the thing they're trying to do versus just optimize for flexibility?
turns.zh: 对于如何让人们使用你的产品并做他们想做的事情而不是仅仅为了灵活性而进行优化，什么时候应该坚持己见，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I think Atlassian built around a process that was already happening and growing momentum and it was like, okay, let's build a solution to enable companies to do this with technology. So there was already a process that didn't have a technology integrated, and then with Greenhouse it was like, there's a better way to do it and this is how it should be done. So I think there's two different approaches. Either find a process that just doesn't have technology that is a best practice or growing best practice. I think the same thing happened in DevOps with many different tools. And then Greenhouse, which is more like, what are companies missing? How can they do it better? How can we train them and teach them a better way? And then by the way, our software helps you do that.
turns.zh: 我认为 Atlassian 是围绕一个已经发生且势头不断增长的流程构建的，就像，好吧，让我们构建一个解决方案，使公司能够利用技术来做到这一点。所以已经有一个没有集成技术的流程，然后使用 Greenhouse 就好像，有更好的方法来做到这一点，这就是应该这样做的方式。所以我认为有两种不同的方法。要么找到一个不具备最佳实践技术的流程，要么不断发展最佳实践。我认为同样的事情也发生在使用许多不同工具的 DevOps 中。然后是 Greenhouse，它更像是，公司缺少什么？他们怎样才能做得更好？我们如何训练他们并教他们更好的方法？顺便说一句，我们的软件可以帮助您做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With the product and company you're building now, are you looking to make it very opinionated and here's how you should be doing performance reviews or how are you thinking about it?
turns.zh: 对于您现在正在构建的产品和公司，您是否希望使其非常固执己见？您应该如何进行绩效评估，或者您是如何考虑的？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yes, we are. It is opinionated, and it's opinionated because the current way that performance reviews happen are full of bias and there's a lot of problems with it. It's like the best thing that companies can do and therefore, they continue to do it, but that just perpetuates a lot of issues. The reason that companies have to go and look at compensation data and fix pay gaps is because they have systemic problems with how people are promoted and progressed in the organization. So if they're recruited in a certain way, they may or may not be developed and then they're evaluated on their performance, which ultimately results in compensation and what people are paid, and that as we know, there's plenty of problems.
turns.zh: 是的，我们是。它是固执己见的，它是固执己见的，因为目前绩效评估的方式充满偏见，而且存在很多问题。这就像公司可以做的最好的事情，因此，他们继续这样做，但这只会使很多问题长期存在。公司之所以必须去查看薪酬数据并解决薪酬差距，是因为他们在组织中如何晋升和进步方面存在系统性问题。因此，如果他们以某种方式招募，他们可能会或可能不会得到发展，然后根据他们的表现进行评估，这最终会导致补偿和人们的报酬，正如我们所知，存在很多问题。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: So companies are fixing this compensation issue by updating the comp every year, but that doesn't fix the systemic problem. And so yes, we have opinions about how to fix the problem and therefore, our building a system that when it comes to performance evaluation, employee progression, we require companies to be more transparent about the levels at the company, the expectations for different levels and competencies, and we create accountability both on the employee and the manager side, but it's also the right thing to do. Employees should feel that they're evaluated fairly, and without a system enforcing some of these things, there's too much subjectivity in the process to make it good, unless you really do a lot of work, which most companies don't do to create the right system. You don't have to use a platform to do it, but if you don't do the work anyway, you won't have the outcome that you want, which is people feeling good about their career and paid fairly.
turns.zh: 因此，公司通过每年更新薪酬来解决这个薪酬问题，但这并不能解决系统性问题。所以，是的，我们对如何解决这个问题有意见，因此，我们建立了一个系统，在绩效评估、员工晋升方面，我们要求公司对公司的级别、对不同级别和能力的期望更加透明，我们在员工和经理方面都建立了问责制，但这也是正确的做法。员工应该感到他们得到了公平的评估，如果没有一个强制执行其中一些事情的系统，那么这个过程中就会有太多的主观性，无法使其变得更好，除非你真的做了很多工作，而大多数公司并没有这样做来创建正确的系统。你不必使用平台来做这件事，但如果你不做这项工作，你就不会得到你想要的结果，即人们对自己的职业感觉良好并且得到公平的报酬。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I found performance reviews to be one of maybe the most powerful tool as a manager to change the way people operate, help them improve, make them fulfilled and happy with where things are going. It feels like that's the core of management, is the performance review cycle and giving people feedback on how they're doing it and then continuing to come back to here's where you're underperforming, here's what it'll take to get to the next level. So I'm excited about what you're working on.
turns.zh: 是的。我发现绩效评估可能是作为管理者最有力的工具之一，可以改变人们的运作方式，帮助他们改进，让他们对事情的进展感到满意和满意。感觉这就是管理的核心，是绩效评估周期，向人们提供有关他们如何做的反馈，然后继续回到这里，看看你表现不佳的地方，这就是达到下一个水平所需要的。所以我对你正在做的事情感到很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've reached our very exciting lightning round where I'm going to ask you five rapid fire questions and you just tell me what comes to mind. We'll go through it pretty fast. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 我们已经进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合，我将快速问你五个问题，你只需告诉我想到的是什么。我们会很快完成它。听起来不错吗？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Awesome. First question, what are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的。惊人的。第一个问题，您最向其他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Definitely Radical Candor. We give this out to customers. It's really good for management and best practices around giving feedback. I love the Art of War just as strategic thinking. And then not work related, a book called Kafka on the Shore. It's one of my favorite Murakami books that I highly recommend.
turns.zh: 绝对是激进的坦诚。我们将其分发给客户。这对于管理和提供反馈的最佳实践确实有好处。我喜欢孙子兵法，就像喜欢战略思维一样。然后是一本与工作无关的书，名叫《海边的卡夫卡》。这是我最喜欢的村上隆的书之一，我强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is that one again?
turns.zh: 那又是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Kafka on the Shore.
turns.zh: 海边的卡夫卡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kafka on the Shore. Wow, cool. I haven't heard of that.
turns.zh: 海边的卡夫卡。哇，酷。我没听说过。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Going to use these in the show notes. What's a favorite other podcast than the one you're currently on?
turns.zh: 惊人的。将在演出笔记中使用这些。除了您当前正在收听的播客之外，您最喜欢的其他播客是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I love Cautionary Tales. I don't know if you know this one, but it's a great podcast that basically identifies and tells stories about the mental mindsets that we're in and the biases that we have and then historic events that have happened and just crazy things that have resulted from things that we do as humans because we're biased.
turns.zh: 我喜欢警世故事。我不知道你是否知道这个，但这是一个很棒的播客，它基本上识别并讲述了我们所处的思维模式和我们所拥有的偏见的故事，然后是已经发生的历史事件，以及我们作为人类因为偏见而所做的事情所导致的疯狂的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Irrational humans.
turns.zh: 非理性的人类。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: It's really good. Yeah.
turns.zh: 真的很好。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite recent movie or a TV show that you watched?
turns.zh: 您最近观看的最喜欢的电影或电视节目是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: I watched Sandman. I don't know if you've heard of this.
turns.zh: 我看了桑德曼。我不知道你是否听说过这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've heard of it. I haven't seen it.
turns.zh: 我听说过。我没见过。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: It's based off of an eight-part graphic novel series by Neil Gaiman. It's really good. The TV version of it isn't exactly about the books, but it's about the characters, and I feel like the way that they portrayed the characters was really interesting and super diverse. It's a great show.
turns.zh: 它改编自尼尔·盖曼的八部分图画小说系列。真的很好。电视剧版并不完全是关于书的，而是关于角色的，我觉得他们描绘角色的方式非常有趣并且非常多样化。这是一场很棒的表演。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's more plus one for that show. What's a favorite interview question that you like to ask when you're interviewing people?
turns.zh: 惊人的。对于那个节目来说，这又是加一。当你面试别人时，你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Everybody hates it, but I like asking what someone's top 10 accomplishments are. They hate it because it's like, "Oh, God. Ugh." But it's really interesting to understand the level of quantitative versus qualitative in their accomplishments, what they value. And also if it's a, "Oh, I ran a hundred miles or I have a great family," whatever it is, it's really interesting to get to know somebody and also what they value.
turns.zh: 每个人都讨厌它，但我喜欢问某人的十大成就是什么。他们讨厌它，因为它就像，“哦，上帝。呃。”但了解他们的成就的定量与定性水平以及他们的价值确实很有趣。而且，如果是“哦，我跑了一百英里，或者我有一个伟大的家庭”，无论是什么，了解某人以及他们的价值观真的很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who else in the industry do you respect most as a thought leader or just influence on your career life?
turns.zh: 作为思想领袖或对您职业生涯的影响，您在行业中最尊敬的还有谁？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Early days, I really appreciated Nancy Duarte. She is based in the Bay Area. She has an agency called Duarte Agency. She does a lot around storytelling and visual communication. She's been really great for me just in my career as a mentor. I've worked with her a couple of times, but also just following all the work that she does. She's amazing.
turns.zh: 早期，我真的很欣赏南希·杜阿尔特。她居住在湾区。她有一个名为杜阿尔特机构的机构。她在讲故事和视觉传达方面做了很多工作。在我作为导师的职业生涯中，她对我来说真的很棒。我曾与她合作过几次，但也只是关注她所做的所有工作。她太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I remember learning about her when Al Gore gave his TED Talk and her whole agency was a-
turns.zh: 惊人的。我记得当阿尔·戈尔 (Al Gore) 发表 TED 演讲时了解到她，她的整个机构都是——

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Yes. She's done an incredible thing with her agency because they started as making presentations more visually appealing, and then it migrated to storytelling, and then it's evolved to change management and how to use story for driving change. And she's also evolved the agency so much over the years as well. She's done a lot of impressive work.
turns.zh: 是的。她与她的机构做了一件令人难以置信的事情，因为他们一开始是让演示文稿在视觉上更具吸引力，然后转向讲故事，然后又发展到变革管理以及如何使用故事来推动变革。多年来，她也使该机构得到了很大的发展。她做了很多令人印象深刻的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Barbra, thank you so much for being here. This was amazing. Two last questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 芭芭拉，非常感谢你来到这里。这太棒了。最后两个问题。如果人们想联系并了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到您？听众如何对您有用？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: LinkedIn is probably the easiest place to find me /BarbraGago. And for me, we're building a product in employee progression, so anybody who wants to share their stories or feedback, our insights around their experiences there or if they're interested in getting product feedback, we're really interested in actual user feedback, even though we're selling to HR teams.
turns.zh: LinkedIn 可能是最容易找到我/BarbraGago 的地方。对我来说，我们正在构建一个关于员工进步的产品，所以任何想要分享他们的故事或反馈、我们对他们在那里的经历的见解的人，或者如果他们有兴趣获得产品反馈，我们真的对实际的用户反馈感兴趣，即使我们是向人力资源团队销售。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what's the URL?
turns.zh: 网址是什么？

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Pando.com.
turns.zh: Pando.com。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Barbra, thank you for being here.
turns.zh: 惊人的。芭芭拉，谢谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Barbra Gago
turns.en: Thank you so much, Lenny.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you so much for listening. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at lennyspodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 非常感谢您的聆听。如果您觉得这很有价值，您可以在 Apple Podcast、Spotify 或您最喜欢的播客应用程序上订阅该节目。另外，请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，因为这确实有助于其他听众找到播客。您可以在 lennyspodcast.com 上找到所有过去的剧集或了解有关该节目的更多信息。下一集见。
